summary: We developed a short stop-motion animation and approached the challenge visually. We created a story about a robot that has to travel to the Moon and Mars to collect ice samples, in order to find out how sustainable its missions and projects are. This matters because it offers a different way to tell the stories of the rovers, and it is a much more educational way to present this information.
details:
PROJECT NAME: Masky

TEAM NAME: CAPS

NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE

DATE: Neiva, November 2026

MAIN FUNCTIONS

Our project is built on three main functions: educational, narrative, and environmental. The short film briefly tells the story of several robots sent by NASA and other space agencies, using both real and fictional data. Our main goal was also to raise awareness among space agencies about the debris that exists today and that will continue to exist far into the future if we do not change the pollution we are leaving behind now.

In addition, drawing on our strengths in storytelling and the arts, our project proposes a short film through which we want to build empathy with the reader and with those who watch the story. Our educational approach is to teach and raise awareness about the history of the rovers sent to the Moon and Mars in a pedagogical way, without it feeling like a class full of figures and scientific data.

HOW IT WORKS

It works through an interactive Canva presentation where you can choose which short film you want to watch first. There are two selectable destinations: the Moon or Mars.

Both destinations share a similar space mission concept, and their acts are also very similar to each other:

ACT 1: MASKY lands on the Moon or on Mars.

ACT 2: It encounters obstacles and the rovers that arrived before it.

ACT 3: The robot reaches two specific locations: on the Moon, Shackleton Crater; on Mars, Hebrus Valles.

ACT 4: It extracts an ice sample from the craters mentioned above.

ACT 5 (FINAL): The samples are sent to Earth for study.

Both share the same ending and mission concept: analyzing ice samples found on Mars and the Moon, but their focuses differ. The purpose of the mission to Mars is to search for life on other planets; on the Moon, the purpose of the mission is to determine whether the water found in that ice is sustainable for building a lunar base with water systems.

OBJECTIVES AND BENEFITS

Our objectives stem from the question posed by the challenge: what happens to the objects sent to and left outside planet Earth? We also seek to show what a robot’s perspective would look like from there, looking at its predecessors, and how technology has evolved with its different capabilities and functions. In addition, we showcase real locations, as well as exploration devices and parts of them. We also make use of free will so that viewers can choose which route they want to watch first.

The benefits are that it can serve as an educational short film for children, because it is one hundred percent animation and uses data provided by NASA about the rovers sent to the Moon and Mars, without necessarily being a documentary that presents the data in a scientific manner.

It can also serve as an environmental awareness short film for space organizations, because of the debris shown in the short film, although this is not our objective within this narrative.

TOOLS USED

As a team, to facilitate the project, we used different software and hardware tools. First, we used several AI chatbots such as Claude, ChatGPT, Meta AI, and, on some occasions, Gemini. We used them both to gather knowledge about NASA and its various rovers, and to improve and assist our project in its different artistic aspects, such as the script, the frames, and the backgrounds. No frame was taken directly from AI; there was always work done entirely by us.

TEHNICAL RESOURCES USED

We used a technique that is one hundred percent handmade, as mentioned above. Our research resources were mostly free AI chatbots: Meta AI, ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. The research on the rovers featured in the film came from Google, using official NASA data and NASA’s AI-assisted research resources, which made it easier to find the information and knowledge we needed for our short film.

REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS

Our short film can be used in children’s education, and it can also inspire other people who want to get closer to NASA, space travel, and the artifacts that have been sent into spac

MASKY SCRIPT

Masky’s story is an educational story built on official data from space organizations, with a touch of fiction.

Two worlds are waiting, and there is only one machine to reach them.

The year is 2187. At a space base on Earth, Masky wakes up, a rover robot like Perseverance.

Its mission: find water. Where there is water, humans can stay.

Masky has two possible destinations: the Moon or Mars. The course of its story depends on what the viewer decides.

Destination 1: The Moon

Mission: search for ice on the Moon and find out how viable it is to build a space base with self-sustaining water systems.

Landing

Masky lands on the Moon.

Right away, it finds trash, but it is not surprised: this is nothing out of the ordinary.

More than one hundred and twenty years of missions have left behind debris that will remain there forever: descent stages, crashed modules, abandoned rovers, landing legs, cables, and sheets of golden insulation.

All of this makes missions like Masky’s more difficult.

The Journey to the Pole

Masky sets off toward the lunar poles, because that is where the possible ice is.

Along the way, debris covers the surface. A sheet of golden insulation tangles around two of its wheels and will not let it move forward.

If it stays stuck, no one will come looking for it.

With its built-in drill, it manages to break free, wheel by wheel.

Those Who Came Before

As it approaches the pole, Masky finds its greatest obstacle: an enormous graveyard of machines.

But it recognizes two that are not trash:

Lunokhod 1: a Soviet rover from 1970 that was lost for decades and located again in 2010.

Pragyan: the rover from India’s Chandrayaan-3 mission, which arrived near the lunar south pole in 2023.

They were here before it.

Shackleton Crater

Masky decides to enter the shadowed crater Shackleton, because it is the most suitable one for a rover like itself:

Energy: its rims receive sunlight for much of the year, so it can charge its batteries and warm up before entering the darkness (verify the percentage).

Signal: from there, there is a good view of Earth, so it can be controlled almost in real time.

Ice: possible ice has been detected in craters that never receive sunlight, although it is still being studied.

But going down has a price. The walls are steep, the battery is low, and the cold is closing in. It must take the sample and return to the light before freezing.

It could stay at the rim, with a full battery and empty hands. Masky decides to go down.

The Sample

Masky ventures into the shadow, collects its ice sample, analyzes it, and sends the results to Earth to be studied.

Then it climbs back toward the light before its battery runs out.

There is ice. There is water.

Whoever comes next deserves a clean path.

Destination 2: Mars

Mission: search for accessible underground ice and study caves, pits, and lava tubes in order to prepare for the arrival of the first astronauts.

Landing

Masky arrives on Mars with the same purpose as on the Moon.

The first things it sees are remains of previous missions: robot parts, heat shields, parachutes, and covers that come off during landing.

This is the landing zone; the place it is looking for is farther away. Masky does not stop and continues with its mission.

The Rover Museum

Along the way, Masky finds a place where several rovers were left abandoned. The first one it recognizes looks like an old microwave:

Sojourner: landed in July 1997 and was the first rover to explore another planet. It is small, but it paved the way. And then

Spirit: landed in 2004 in Gusev Crater, worked for more than six years, and found evidence of hydrothermal activity and ancient water.

Curiosity: said to be its older brother, a mobile laboratory the size of a car that landed in 2012 in Gale Crater. And finally,

Zhurong: a Chinese rover that landed in 2021 in Utopia Planitia, with a mission similar to Masky’s: to study the subsurface.

They are not trash. They are the ones who arrived first.

The Radar

Masky uses its RIMFAX ground-penetrating radar to search for ice beneath the ground. A radar in orbit helps pinpoint the zones, and RIMFAX explores them up close.

This is how it reaches Hebrus Valles, a region with pits or skylights, possible underground ice at shallow depth, and nearby volcanic tubes (verify).

There, a habitat protected from radiation could be built, with water, oxygen, and fuel just a few meters away.

Virgin Terrain

Unlike the landing zone, here the terrain is untouched, with no trash and no contamination.

Masky is the first rover to set foot in this region. Nothing blocks its way, but now the challenge is a different one.

This is a region without footprints.

The Pit

Masky ventures into a pit with steep walls, fractured rocks, and overhanging ceilings. The atmosphere is sinister, and moving among the rocks scattered across the ground is laborious.

Suddenly, a rock breaks loose from the ceiling and falls very close by. One of its wheels slips.

If a rock falls on it, no one will know it was ever there. But it is already there.

The Sample

Despite the difficulties, Masky collects its ice sample, analyzes it, and sends the results to Earth to be studied.

Ice, just a few meters below the surface.

Someone has to be the first.

Closing

(Shown after either of the two destinations.)

Masky’s results arrive on Earth.

Two worlds, one same question: how can we live far from home without leaving behind in our wake what we cannot repair?

On the Moon, trash gets in the way. On Mars, the path is still clean.

Masky did not choose where to go. You did.
